name: Gaucher Disease

prevalence.estimate: 1 in 40,000 to 1 in 60,000 (general); 1 in 800 in Ashkenazi Jewish population

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Expert consensus guidelines for Gaucher disease diagnosis

criteria.description: Deficient acid beta-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase) activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts (<15% of normal)
Biallelic pathogenic variants in GBA1 gene
Gaucher cells on bone marrow biopsy (lipid-laden macrophages with crinkled tissue paper appearance)
Hepatosplenomegaly with cytopenia(s) on clinical examination and laboratory evaluation

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Deficient glucocerebrosidase enzyme activity, confirmed by GBA1 genetic testing. Enzyme assay is the gold standard.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Type 1 (non-neuronopathic, ~94%) is most common and does not involve the CNS. Type 2 (acute neuronopathic) is fatal in infancy. Type 3 (chronic neuronopathic) has variable neurological involvement. GBA1 mutations are a strong risk factor for Parkinson disease.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Gaucher cells on bone marrow biopsy
pathognomonic.notes: Lipid-laden macrophages with characteristic 'crinkled tissue paper' or 'wrinkled silk' cytoplasm; not entirely specific as pseudo-Gaucher cells can occur in other conditions

common.notes: Spleen may enlarge 5-75x normal; most consistent finding in type 1
Due to hypersplenism and marrow infiltration
Acute bone crises mimic osteomyelitis; chronic bone pain also common

occasional.symptomName: Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur
occasional.notes: Failure of normal cortical bone remodeling

rare.notes: GBA1 heterozygotes and homozygotes have increased Parkinson disease risk
Hallmark of type 3; horizontal supranuclear gaze palsy

laboratory: Deficient acid beta-glucosidase (glucocerebrosidase) enzyme activity (<15% of normal)
Markedly elevated plasma glucosylsphingosine (lyso-Gb1) - sensitive and specific biomarker
Elevated serum chitotriosidase (6-null genotype in ~6% of population limits utility)
Elevated serum ferritin, elevated ACE level (nonspecific)
imaging: MRI of femurs and spine showing bone marrow infiltration (T1 low signal, T2 variable)
X-ray showing Erlenmeyer flask deformity of distal femur
MRI or ultrasound showing hepatosplenomegaly with volumetric measurements
DEXA scan showing osteopenia or osteoporosis
MRI showing avascular necrosis or bone infarcts
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in GBA1 gene (chromosome 1q22)
N370S (N409S) most common mutation in type 1 (precludes type 2/3 if homozygous)
L444P (L483P) associated with more severe disease and neuronopathic forms
84GG insertion common in Ashkenazi Jewish population
GBA1 carrier status is strongest genetic risk factor for Parkinson disease
other: Bone marrow biopsy showing Gaucher cells (supportive but not required; avoid pseudo-Gaucher cells)
Dried blood spot testing for enzyme activity (screening)
Bone density assessment (DEXA and quantitative CT)

distinguishingFeatures: Niemann-Pick has foamy storage cells rather than crinkled tissue paper cells
Niemann-Pick type A/B involves acid sphingomyelinase deficiency
Cherry red spot present in Niemann-Pick type A
Leukemia shows blast cells on peripheral smear and bone marrow
Leukemia may cause similar hepatosplenomegaly and cytopenias
Fabry is X-linked, not autosomal recessive
ITP has isolated thrombocytopenia without hepatosplenomegaly
Normal enzyme activity and biomarkers in ITP

redFlags: Type 2 (acute neuronopathic) presentation in infancy with bulbar signs and rapid deterioration
Massive splenomegaly with risk of splenic rupture
Acute bone crisis mimicking osteomyelitis (requires differentiation)
Pulmonary hypertension (serious complication, may not respond to ERT alone)
Development of Parkinson disease symptoms in Gaucher patients or carriers
references: Biegstraaten M, et al. Management goals for type 1 Gaucher disease: An expert consensus document. Blood Cells Mol Dis. 2018;68:203-208.

Sidransky E, et al. Multicenter analysis of glucocerebrosidase mutations in Parkinson's disease. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(17):1651-61.
